claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9457 s3: "The canonical model for problem details is a JSON object. When serialized in a JSON document, that format is identified with the \"application/problem+json\" media type." s3.1 lists exactly five members (type, status, title, detail, instance) and opens with "Problem detail objects CAN HAVE the following members"; Appendix A's schema declares no "required" list. But s1 also says: "problem details are (naturally) not the only way to convey the details of a problem in HTTP" and "defined HTTP status codes cover many situations with no need to convey extra detail."
claim_verdicts.source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457 s1, s3, s3.1, Appendix A
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: RFC 9457 defines the Problem Details JSON object (media type application/problem+json) with five optional members — type, title, status, detail, instance — plus API-defined extension members. It is a standard error format for HTTP APIs, not the only permitted one.

claim_verdicts.evidence: RFC 9457 s3.1.1: "When this member is not present, its value is assumed to be \"about:blank\"." s4.2.1: "The \"about:blank\" URI, when used as a problem type, indicates that the problem has no additional semantics beyond that of the HTTP status code." and "any problem details object not carrying an explicit \"type\" member implicitly uses this URI."

RFC 9457 s3.1.2: "The \"status\" member is a JSON number indicating the HTTP status code generated by the origin server for this occurrence of the problem." and "The \"status\" member, if present, is only advisory; it conveys the HTTP status code used for the convenience of the consumer. Generators MUST use the same status code in the actual HTTP response." Note the "only advisory" qualifier, which the claim and the lesson both drop (see issue on s4).

claim_verdicts.source: examples/don-hang @ stage-0: Caddyfile:80-82; live curl on the running lab

claim_verdicts.evidence: The supporting sentence is in s1, not the abstract: "Problem details can be used with any HTTP status code, but they most naturally fit the semantics of 4xx and 5xx responses." The abstract says only "to carry machine-readable details of errors in HTTP response content" — nothing about status classes. Grep of the full RFC text for "503" returns zero hits; the worked examples use 403 Forbidden (s3) and 422 Unprocessable Content (s3), i.e. two client errors, not "403 and 503".
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: RFC 9457 s1: "Problem details can be used with any HTTP status code, but they most naturally fit the semantics of 4xx and 5xx responses" — so 4xx responses are not exempt. Its worked examples use 403 and 422, both client errors.

claim_verdicts.evidence:
Ran `curl -sS -i http://localhost:8080/conflict` against the running lab. Output:
HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Server: Caddy
Date: Thu, 24 Sep 2026 17:53:26 GMT
Content-Length: 37

Conflict: this order was already paid
Matches the claim and the lesson's "Expected result" on every point: status, Content-Type, length, exact body, no JSON, no error field.

issues.quote: the standard JSON shape for an error response: a body with `type`, `title`, `status`, and `detail`
issues.text: The lesson presents Problem Details as exactly four fields, in s3, s4 ("every one of them returns the same four fields"), s5 ("the same four fields, no matter which endpoint") and s9. RFC 9457 s3.1 defines five members — the fifth is `instance` — plus extension members (s3.2), and Appendix A's schema requires none of them. The ledger's claim 1 itself writes "(plus instance, not covered here)", but no sentence in the lesson carries that qualifier, so a junior meeting a real Problem Details body with `instance` or an extension will read it as non-conforming.
issues.fix: In s3 write: "a standard JSON shape for an error response; this lesson uses four of its fields — `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`". Add one sentence at the end of s3: "RFC 9457 defines one more field, `instance`, and lets an API add fields of its own — a body with extra fields is still Problem Details." Replace "the same four fields" with "the same fields" in s4, s5 and s9 point 1/5.

issues.quote: `type` — a short, stable identifier for the kind of problem
issues.text: Unlisted claim and an inaccurate one. RFC 9457 s3.1.1: "The \"type\" member is a JSON string containing a URI reference that identifies the problem type. Consumers MUST use the \"type\" URI (after resolution, if necessary) as the problem type's primary identifier", and "it is RECOMMENDED that absolute URIs be used in \"type\" when possible". "A short identifier" invites a junior to write `"type": "order not found"` — a string with a space, not a URI reference. No claim in the ledger covers what `type` must contain.
issues.fix: Reword to: "`type` — a URI reference that identifies the kind of problem; it is an identifier, not a sentence, and stays the same for every response of that kind." Add a claim (kind `syntax`, version_key `http_problem_details`, source_hint "RFC 9457 s3.1.1") recording that `type` holds a URI reference.

issues.quote: `type` and `title` describe the *kind* of problem, so they stay the same on every response for that kind
issues.text: Unlisted claim. The per-occurrence semantics of `title` and `detail` are asserted three times (s3 "the same text every time this kind of error happens", s4, s9 point 3) and quiz q3 keys on them, yet no claim in the ledger covers them. The wording is also absolute where the RFC is not — s3.1.3: "It SHOULD NOT change from occurrence to occurrence of the problem, except for localization"; s4.2.1 repeats that a title "MAY be localized to suit client preferences".
issues.fix: Add a claim (kind `fact`, version_key `http_problem_details`, source_hint "RFC 9457 s3.1.3 title, s3.1.4 detail") for the fixed-vs-per-occurrence split. In s3 change "the same text every time this kind of error happens" to "meant to read the same on every occurrence of this kind of error (it may be translated for the reader)".

issues.quote: A `400` still means the request itself was wrong, a `404` still means nothing matches, a `409` still means a conflict with the resource's current state
issues.text: Unlisted claim: three status-code definitions, none in the ledger. `versions_used` lists `http`, but not a single claim carries `version_key: http` — the version is declared and never anchored. RFC 9110 s15.5.5 also defines 404 more narrowly than "nothing matches": "the origin server did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists" — a 404 can be a deliberate refusal to disclose.
issues.fix: Add one claim (kind `fact`, version_key `http`, source_hint "RFC 9110 s15.5.1, s15.5.5, s15.5.10") covering the three codes. Reword the 404 clause to "a `404` still means the server has no current representation for that resource".

issues.quote: `GET /api/v1/orders/999` returns `404` with the body `{"error":"order not found"}` — the lab's fixed stand-in for a real endpoint
issues.text: Present tense about "the lab", but this lesson is stage 1 and the example repo has moved on: at HEAD (post stage-1) the Caddyfile has no `@missingOrder` handler at all — `/api/v1/orders/*` is proxied to the real API, which answers with Problem Details. The quoted body is true only of tag stage-0. s7 compounds it: "With the stage-0 lab running (`scripts/up.sh`)" — `scripts/up.sh` in a stage-1 checkout starts the stage-1 lab, not a stage-0 one. A reader who ignores "without curling it again" sees the lesson contradicted.
issues.fix: s2: "At stage-0 the lab answered `GET /api/v1/orders/999` with `404` and the body `{\"error\":\"order not found\"}` — a fixed stand-in for a real endpoint." s7 step 1: drop "stage-0" — "With the lab running (`scripts/up.sh`), run `curl -sS -i http://localhost:8080/conflict`" (verified live: `/conflict` is unchanged). s7 step 2: "Compare it to the stage-0 `/api/v1/orders/999` handler quoted above — don't curl that path, the lab no longer serves the fixed body."

issues.quote: code that has already deserialized the body into an object can still tell which HTTP status caused it, without also holding on to the raw response
issues.text: True as far as it goes (RFC 9457 s3.1.2 gives exactly this rationale: consumers can use it "when a message's content is persisted without HTTP information"), but the lesson drops the qualifier in the preceding sentence of the same section: "The \"status\" member, if present, is only advisory... Generic HTTP software will still use the HTTP status code." Quiz q4 option d trains the same habit, so a junior can end up branching on the body's number instead of the response's.
issues.fix: Append to that sentence: "— the status line is still the authoritative one; the body's `status` is a copy kept for convenience."

issues.quote: Caddy's respond directive defaults to text/plain for a plain string
issues.text: Claim 5 asserts Caddy behaviour but carries no `version_key`, so nothing pins it to caddy 2.10 even though `versions_used` lists `caddy`. It is confirmed here only by execution against the running lab, not by any Caddy document I opened.
issues.fix: Add `"version_key": "caddy"` to claim 5 in `.meta.json` (and to claim 7, which observes the same Content-Type live), so a future caddy bump re-triggers review per versions.yaml policy line 3.

issues.quote: Put these four facts about a failing request in the order they happen
issues.text: The key `a, b, c, d` is defensible only because s4 says `status` "copies the exact number already sitting on the response's status line". In endpoint code the body object is usually built before anything is written to the wire, so a reader reasoning about their own code can argue c before b. The question stem ("from the endpoint's code running") points at code, while the key's order is the wire order.
issues.fix: Change option b to "The response's status line goes out carrying the code `404`" and option c to "The response body that follows it is a Problem Details object, with `status` set to that same number", so the wire ordering is explicit in the options.
